Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-47101", "CVE-2026-47102", "CVE-2026-40217", "CVE-2026-42271")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-47101", "CVE-2026-47102", "CVE-2026-40217", "CVE-2026-42271")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\regsvr32.exe'

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Popular WordPress Plugin Scripts Tampered to Plant Hidden Backdoors on Sites

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An attacker tampered with trusted JavaScript files used by WordPress sites running PushEngage, OptinMonster, and TrustPulse, turning those files into a way to break into the sites. When a site administrator was logged in as the file loaded, the code created an admin account under the attacker's control and installed a hidden plugin that opened a way back in. Ordinary visitors did not trigger it

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Admin browser loaded poisoned PushEngage CDN script during exposure window
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Web server PHP runtime spawning a shell (WordPress web shell execution) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Popular WordPress Plugin Scripts Tampered to Plant Hidden Backdoors on Sites
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hidden WordPress backdoor plugin dropped (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer) · [LLM] Rogue WordPress administrator account (developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx) · [LLM] WordPress plugin/theme PHP files modified by the web runtime (backdoor / skimmer injection)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Rogue admin & self-hiding plugin C2/exfil to tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Rogue admin & self-hiding plugin C2/exfil to tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the campaign's command-and-control / credential-exfil leg: any host or web server reaching the attacker lookalike domain tidio[.]cc (including its /cdn-cgi/ paths) or the C2 IP 84.201.6.54, to which the poisoned plugin scripts ship the freshly created admin credentials and site info. tidio[.]cc is a confirmed-malicious lookalike of tidio.com registered weeks before the attack, so any contact is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the two highest-fidelity network IOCs in the article — the lookalike C2 domain tidio[.]cc and IP 84.201.6.54 — both independently confirmed by Sansec, Patchstack and BleepingComputer. Any contact is malicious because tidio[.]cc is a fake registered 2026-04-28 to impersonate tidio.com. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://patchstack.com/articles/supply-chain-attack-on-optinmonster-trustpulse-and-pushengage-tampered-cdn-scripts-auto-creating-rogue-admins/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/optinmonster-wordpress-plugin-hacked-in-cdn-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user genuinely typo-visiting tidio.cc in a browser rather than the real tidio.com chat product
  • Threat-intel sandbox / security researcher detonating the sample from a corporate egress IP
  • Passive DNS or URL-scanning service on the network resolving the IOC for reputation checks
  • Another tenant/host legitimately renting 84.201.6.54 from Ultahost after the campaign (re-validate WHOIS/reputation before action)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/server reaching tidio.cc or 84.201.6.54 and the initiating process — a php/web-server process or admin browser strongly confirms compromise. 2) Contain: block tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54 at proxy/firewall/DNS sinkhole, isolate the affected web server, and force-rotate the WordPress admin passwords, salts (wp-config.php), DB and CDN credentials. 3) Hunt: server-side scan for the hidden plugin folders content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer and rogue admins developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx; review web access logs June 12-14 UTC for /cdn-cgi/ paths to tidio.cc.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tidio.cc" or RemoteIP == "84.201.6.54"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has "tidio.cc" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator = Name, Kind = "DNS"),
  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "84.201.6.54" or Url has "tidio.cc" | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Indicator = coalesce(Url, DstIpAddr), Kind = "Network")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hidden WordPress backdoor plugin dropped (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer) AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-disk persistence artifact: creation of the attacker's self-hiding plugin directories 'content-delivery-helper' (Content Delivery Helper) or 'database-optimizer' (Database Optimizer) under wp-content/plugins. These directories hold the web shell and are invisible from the WordPress dashboard, so the only reliable detection is on the filesystem. Rationale: Anchored on the two exact backdoor plugin slugs named in Sansec's IOCs (content-delivery-helper, database-optimizer) under wp-content/plugins — these directory names are not legitimate WordPress/Awesome Motive plugins, making their appearance a near-certain compromise indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://patchstack.com/articles/supply-chain-attack-on-optinmonster-trustpulse-and-pushengage-tampered-cdn-scripts-auto-creating-rogue-admins/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin coincidentally naming a custom in-house plugin folder 'database-optimizer' (verify author headers and file contents)
  • A backup/restore or staging-sync tool recreating the directory while operators are remediating
  • Security tooling quarantining/copying the malicious folder to a new path during cleanup
  • A different legitimate marketplace plugin that happens to ship a 'content-delivery-helper' subfolder (inspect the plugin main file header)
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped directory's main PHP file and check for web-shell / eval / base64_decode patterns and the absence of a legitimate plugin header. 2) Contain: take the site offline or into maintenance, remove the plugin folder, and treat the host as fully compromised — rotate all WordPress, DB, CDN and salt credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate all admin users for developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx, search web logs for tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54, and scan for additional web shells since the actor had arbitrary code execution.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath contains "content-delivery-helper" or FolderPath contains "database-optimizer"
| where FolderPath contains "wp-content"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath contains "wp-content"
| where TargetFilePath contains "content-delivery-helper" or TargetFilePath contains "database-optimizer"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

      - 'wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper'
      - 'wp-content\plugins\content-delivery-helper'

  condition: selection

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*content-delivery-helper* OR @TargetFilename:*database-optimizer* OR @TargetFilename:*Content-Delivery-Helper* OR @TargetFilename:*Database-Optimizer*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/wp-content.plugins.(content-delivery-helper|database-optimizer)/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*content-delivery-helper*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*database-optimizer*") by _time, Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*content-delivery-helper*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*database-optimizer*") by _time, Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - _time
Rogue WordPress administrator account (developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the campaign's privilege-escalation/persistence step: creation of an attacker-controlled administrator whose username is developer_api1 or matches the dev_xxxxxx pattern. Surfaces the account name wherever it appears in web-server process command lines (e.g. wp-cli, direct SQL inserts) or WordPress audit/security-plugin logs. Rationale: Uses the exact rogue-account names Sansec told operators to delete — developer_api1 and the dev_xxxxxx pattern — combined with account-creation context so the match is specific to attacker-driven WordPress admin provisioning rather than generic user management. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://patchstack.com/articles/supply-chain-attack-on-optinmonster-trustpulse-and-pushengage-tampered-cdn-scripts-auto-creating-rogue-admins/
ATT&CKT1136 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate developer/service account genuinely named 'developer_api1' provisioned by the site team
  • An admin running wp-cli to audit or list users where the name appears in a benign command
  • A migration/seed script referencing the string in test fixtures
  • WordPress security plugin (Wordfence/WP Activity Log) echoing the IOC name back in an informational alert about the attack itself
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("wpactivitylog","wordfence") and ProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the account exists in wp_users and check its registration timestamp against the June 12-14 window and whether anyone owns it. 2) Contain: delete the rogue admin (and any dev_xxxxxx siblings), invalidate all active sessions/auth cookies, and rotate admin passwords and wp-config salts. 3) Hunt: because deleting the account alone is insufficient, also remove the hidden plugin folders, search egress for tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54, and scan for additional persistence the web shell may have planted.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "developer_api1" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)dev_[a-z0-9]{6}"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("user create","wp user","wp_users","INSERT INTO","role=administrator","role administrator")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "developer_api1" or SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)dev_[a-z0-9]{6}"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("user_register","wp_insert_user","create_user","Administrator","role")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(developer_api1|dev_[a-z0-9]{6})/i
| CommandLine=/(user.create|wp.user|wp_users|role.{0,3}administrator|insert.into)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*developer_api1*" OR Processes.process="*dev_*") (Processes.process="*user create*" OR Processes.process="*wp_users*" OR Processes.process="*role=administrator*" OR Processes.process="*INSERT INTO*") by _time, Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*developer_api1*" OR Processes.process="*dev_*") (Processes.process="*user create*" OR Processes.process="*wp_users*" OR Processes.process="*role=administrator*" OR Processes.process="*INSERT INTO*") by _time, Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - _time
Web server PHP runtime spawning a shell (WordPress web shell execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the hidden backdoor plugin's web shell executing OS commands: a PHP/web-server process (php-fpm, php.exe, httpd, apache2, nginx, w3wp) spawning cmd, powershell, sh or bash. Web servers almost never spawn interactive shells, so this parent→child chain is a high-fidelity sign of code execution via the planted web shell. Rationale: Targets the described web-shell capability ('run code on the server without logging in') via the parent→child shape that legitimate WordPress hosting never produces — the PHP/web runtime spawning an interactive shell — making it article-specific to the backdoor's execution stage without relying on generic interpreter detection. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/optinmonster-wordpress-plugin-hacked-in-cdn-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress/PHP deployment or update hooks that shell out to run composer/git/wp-cli
  • A monitoring or backup plugin that invokes mysqldump or tar via shell_exec
  • Sysadmin running a PHP maintenance script interactively from the web user
  • CI/CD agent on the web host invoking shell builds under the web-server service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","composer","mysqldump","--version") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "vendor")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the PHP script path/PID that initiated it; a base64/eval-laden or recon command (whoami, id, uname) confirms a web shell. 2) Contain: isolate the web server, kill the offending PHP worker, and block egress to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54. 3) Hunt: locate the originating PHP file (likely in content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer), enumerate all files it touched, check for rogue admins and additional web shells, and rotate all credentials.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Child = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Server PHP Process Spawning Shell (WordPress Web Shell)
id: 8a1f0b22-3c4d-4e5f-9a6b-7c8d9e0f1a2b
description: Detects a PHP/web-server runtime spawning an OS shell, indicative of web-shell command execution from the planted WordPress backdoor plugin.
references:
  - https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:

  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '\php.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/nginx'
      - '\w3wp.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\php.exe OR *\PHP.exe OR *\php-cgi.exe OR *\httpd.exe OR *\w3wp.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(php|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp)/i
| ImageFileName=/.(cmd|powershell|pwsh|sh|bash|dash|wscript|cscript)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")) (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) by _time, Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")) (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) by _time, Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - _time
WordPress plugin/theme PHP files modified by the web runtime (backdoor / skimmer injection) AIInstallation Medium
Behavioral hunt for post-compromise file tampering described in the article — the actor can 'read or change any file, plant more backdoors, inject card-skimming code.' Surfaces .php files under wp-content/plugins, wp-content/themes, wp-includes or wp-admin being written by the PHP/web-server runtime, then aggregates by host and writer process so analysts can spot anomalous bursts of code changes. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit post-exploitation capability (plant more backdoors / inject card-skimming code / change any file): scopes to WordPress code directories and requires the PHP/web runtime as the writer so it catches web-shell-driven tampering rather than every file change. Hunting tier because WordPress auto-updates also write via php-fpm. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://patchstack.com/articles/supply-chain-attack-on-optinmonster-trustpulse-and-pushengage-tampered-cdn-scripts-auto-creating-rogue-admins/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress core/plugin/theme auto-updates writing PHP via php-fpm
  • An admin editing theme/plugin code through the built-in WordPress file editor
  • A caching or optimization plugin generating advanced-cache.php / object-cache.php drop-ins
  • Deployment automation (Composer, wp-cli, rsync) refreshing plugin code during a release window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp plugin update","wp core update","wp theme update","--update"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the modified PHP files for eval/base64_decode/gzinflate/preg_replace-e and external POST calls; correlate the write time with any scheduled plugin-update activity. 2) Contain: if malicious, restore the file from a known-good source or backup, isolate the host, and rotate credentials and salts. 3) Hunt: pivot from the writer process to all files it touched, check for the hidden plugin folders and rogue admins, and look for egress to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("wp-content","wp-includes","wp-admin")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| summarize Writes = count(), Files = make_set(FolderPath, 50), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Last desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("wp-content","wp-includes","wp-admin")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| summarize Writes = count(), Files = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by Last desc

Admin browser loaded poisoned PushEngage CDN script during exposure window AIDelivery Medium
Retro-exposure hunt to scope which sites/admins pulled the tampered PushEngage embeds (pushengage-web-sdk.js / pushengage-subscription.js) from clientcdn.pushengage.com during the June 12-14 2026 UTC window. Because the dashboard cannot reveal compromise, this answers the prerequisite question 'were our admins served the poisoned script?' to prioritize server-side scans. Rationale: Uses the exact poisoned filenames (pushengage-web-sdk.js, pushengage-subscription.js) and CDN host (clientcdn.pushengage.com) plus the article's June 12-14 UTC window to scope exposure. Confidence/FP reflect that this measures reach, not damage — a load only matters if a logged-in admin triggered it — so it feeds server-side scanning rather than alerting on its own. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/optinmonster-wordpress-plugin-hacked-in-cdn-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate PushEngage user loaded the same host/filenames during the window — most hits are benign reach, not compromise
  • Non-admin visitor sessions where the dormant payload never fired
  • Synthetic monitoring / uptime checks fetching site pages that embed the script
  • CDN edge caches returning a clean copy after Awesome Motive replaced the files mid-window
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each host that loaded the script, determine whether the session belonged to a logged-in WordPress administrator (the only condition under which the payload executes). 2) Contain: for confirmed admin loads, run an immediate server-side scan and treat the site as compromised pending results. 3) Hunt: on flagged sites, check for content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer plugin folders, developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx admins, and egress to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54; rotate all secrets if any are found.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-14T23:59:59Z))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "clientcdn.pushengage.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp asc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-14T23:59:59Z))
| where Url has "clientcdn.pushengage.com"
| where Url has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated asc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-10795")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-10795")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("84.201.6.54") or RemoteUrl has_any ("tidio.cc", "pushengage.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EvilTokens device-code token polling from attacker infra (python-requests UA / C2 IPs) · [LLM] EvilTokens device-code lure email (Acrobat/DocuSign decoy, 'Verify to view') · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Microsoft 365 OAuth device code authentication flow sign-in (EvilTokens) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-device-code malicious inbox rule creation (BEC prep) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Microsoft 365 OAuth device code authentication flow sign-in (EvilTokens) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow — the exact mechanism EvilTokens abuses to have a victim authorize the attacker's session on the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page. In tenants that don't legitimately use device code flow, any occurrence is a strong account-takeover indicator. Rationale: Anchors on the OAuth device code grant — the single behaviour that defines EvilTokens — surfaced via the AuthenticationProcessingDetails 'Device Code' marker (Defender/Sentinel) and AuthenticationProtocol=deviceCode (Sigma). Microsoft and Sekoia both confirm deviceCode/originalTransferMethod fields are the primary detection surface and are absent from normal interactive sign-ins. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-oauth-device-code-phishing-m365-20260325-c/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running 'az login --use-device-code' from a workstation
  • Sysadmin connecting Microsoft Graph PowerShell with -UseDeviceAuthentication
  • Conference-room / smart-TV / kiosk device enrollment using device code
  • Legacy line-of-business app onboarded via device code grant
  • Help-desk provisioning a shared device on behalf of a user
Suppression filter
| where tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).trustType) !in ("Azure AD joined", "Hybrid Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sign-in's IPAddress, UserAgent, AppDisplayName and DeviceTrust. Managed/compliant device + corporate IP + Azure CLI/PowerShell app = likely admin self-service; unmanaged device + VPS/residential-proxy IP + python-requests UA = treat as compromise. 2) Contain: if suspicious, revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and require re-MFA. 3) Hunt: review the same user's subsequent mailbox access, new inbox rules, OneDrive/SharePoint downloads, and any Teams/Graph activity from the same IP in the following 72h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| extend DeviceTrust = tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).trustType)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrust, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code token polling from attacker infra (python-requests UA / C2 IPs) AIDelivery Medium
Detects device-code sign-ins originating from the EvilTokens C2 IP ranges or carrying the python-requests user-agent characteristic of the kit's token-polling loop against Microsoft's devicecode endpoint. This is the attacker's authenticating 'device' picking up access/refresh tokens after the victim enters the code. Rationale: Combines the corroborated device-code protocol with two high-fidelity discriminators: the python-requests token-polling user-agent (named in Microsoft's Storm-2372 analysis) and the article's EvilTokens IP ranges (treated as /24 from the .0 IOCs). The TTP+UA pair is cross-confirmed; the specific IPs are article-sourced enrichment. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Python automation/script using device code flow against Graph (uncommon)
  • Security scanner or red-team tooling emulating device code phishing
  • Shared NAT egress where a single corporate IP overlaps a flagged hosting range (unlikely for the listed VPS blocks)
  • Pen-test of conditional access device-code policy
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the AccountUpn, the AppDisplayName the token was minted for, and whether the source IP is a known VPS/hosting block; python-requests + device code is effectively never benign for end-user accounts. 2) Contain: immediately revoke sessions and refresh tokens for the account, disable the account if active mailbox/Graph access is seen, and add the IP ranges to a block/Conditional-Access named location. 3) Hunt: sweep all other accounts that authenticated from the same IPs in the last 30 days, and pivot to OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents for inbox-rule creation and mass downloads.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests"
    or ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "162.220.232.0/24", "162.220.234.0/24", "89.150.45.0/24", "185.81.113.0/24")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ErrorCode, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests"
    or ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "162.220.232.0/24", "162.220.234.0/24", "89.150.45.0/24", "185.81.113.0/24")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ResultType, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code lure email (Acrobat/DocuSign decoy, 'Verify to view') AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound mail delivering the EvilTokens lure — links to the kit's decoy domains or subjects impersonating document/signature/calendar requests that route the victim toward microsoft.com/devicelogin. Targets the delivery step before the victim ever enters the attacker's code. Rationale: Pivots on the kit's named decoy domains (authdocspro/docusend impersonating DocuSign, eventcalender-schedule for the calendar-invite lure) plus the article's verbatim lure strings 'Verify to view' / 'Signature required', combined with a devicelogin URL target. Domains are article-sourced; the Acrobat/DocuSign decoy theme is corroborated by Sekoia. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine DocuSign/Adobe Acrobat Sign notification with a 'Signature required' subject
  • Legitimate SharePoint/OneDrive 'shared a document' invite
  • Internal calendar-invite tooling using 'Verify to access' language
  • Marketing/e-sign vendor newsletters that happen to contain the lure phrasing
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the sending domain's SPF/DKIM/DMARC and the UrlDomain reputation; a freshly-registered look-alike (authdocspro, docusend.networkssolutionmail) routing to devicelogin is high-confidence phishing. 2) Contain: ZAP/soft-delete the message across all recipients, block the sender + URL domains at the secure email gateway, and warn recipients not to enter any code. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents for recipients who clicked, then correlate to SigninLogs for any device-code sign-in by those users within 15 minutes (the code's validity window).

Post-device-code malicious inbox rule creation (BEC prep) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a recent device-code sign-in by a user with that same user creating an auto-delete/forward/move inbox rule — the EvilTokens post-compromise pattern where attackers hide replies and stage BEC. Ties two telemetry sources to cut the noise of routine rule changes. Rationale: Gates the well-known malicious-inbox-rule signal behind a recent device-code sign-in by the same identity, making it specific to the EvilTokens account-takeover chain rather than a generic rule-change hunt. The hide/forward parameter keywords match the article's 'new inbox rules' warning and corroborated BEC staging behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User who legitimately enrolled a device via device code then set up a normal folder-organization rule
  • Admin/help-desk creating delegate or archive rules on a mailbox
  • Outlook 'sweep'/clutter rule auto-moving newsletters to a folder
  • Legitimate auto-forward to a personal-archive mailbox approved by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "DeleteMessage", "Deleted Items", "RSS Feeds"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the rule's Parameters/RawEventData — forwarding to an external address or moving replies to RSS Feeds/Deleted Items/Archive is hostile; benign rules sort known senders into named folders. 2) Contain: delete the malicious inbox rule, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, reset credentials, and disable external auto-forwarding tenant-wide if not required. 3) Hunt: review Sent Items and OfficeActivity for outbound BEC messages, check whether finance/HR/AP counterparties were contacted, and pivot on the sign-in IP to find other compromised mailboxes.
let DeviceCodeUsers = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
    | distinct AccountObjectId;

| where ActionType in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")

| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "Deleted Items", "Junk Email", "RSS Feeds", "Archive", "MarkAsRead")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCodeUsers = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| where UserId in~ (DeviceCodeUsers)
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "Deleted Items", "Junk Email", "RSS Feeds", "Archive", "MarkAsRead")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Parameters, OriginatingServer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
